title: GCD and LCM Calculator
story: You're tiling a floor with square tiles of equal size. The room is 48 by 18 feet. What's the largest square tile that fits perfectly? That's GCD — greatest common divisor. What's the smallest room size that fits both 48ft and 18ft tiles? That's LCM. Ancient Greek math, modern code.
why: GCD and LCM are foundational algorithms used everywhere from cryptography to computer graphics. The Euclidean algorithm for GCD is one of the oldest algorithms still in use.
analogy: GCD is like finding the largest measuring cup that exactly fills two containers without leaving leftover water. LCM is finding the smallest container that both measuring cups can fill exactly. Two sides of the same coin, connected by a simple formula.
try_it: Compute GCD and LCM for pairs of large prime numbers — the GCD should be 1. Compute GCD of (100, 0) — what happens? Add a contract that requires both inputs to be positive. Test with (1071, 462) — GCD should be 21.
tips: Divide first then multiply for LCM: (a / gcd) * b avoids overflow
The Euclidean algorithm is O(log n) — extremely fast for any numbers
GCD of two primes is always 1 — they share no common factors
common_mistakes: Computing LCM as (a * b) / gcd — this can overflow for large numbers
Swapping the assignment order in the GCD loop — temp must catch y first
